With the launch of the M6 Mac mini and its more powerful M5 Pro counterpart, Apple has quietly killed one of the most appealing features of this computer. Although the two new Mac minis look almost identical to the previous generation from the outside, Apple has removed a hidden feature that made the previous Mac mini exceptionally good value for money.

When the M4 Mac mini first launched, its value for money was remarkable. It came not only with the Apple M4 SoC, but also with a generous 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, as well as HDMI and Ethernet. Starting at the original price of $599 USD or $499 USD for students, the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac in Apple's range, but the best Mac at its price point.

Video: Apple Killed the Mac mini's Best Hidden Feature :(

However, this smallest Mac from Apple actually had a hidden trick up its sleeve that took its value to another level: it featured a slot for upgradeable storage. Users could literally open the bottom cover on the back, unscrew a few screws, and access a removable NAND module that could easily be swapped out for a third-party SSD of up to 2TB.

The benefits were manifold. Not only could you upgrade the SSD, or easily repair a damaged drive, but by foregoing Apple's factory upgrade options and installing a cheaper third-party SSD yourself, you could save a considerable amount of money.

At the time, Apple priced the 2TB upgrade at $800 USD, meaning this 'budget' computer could quickly turn into a $1,400 USD machine with just one checkbox ticked. If users opted to upgrade with a third-party SSD after purchase, they could save close to $500 USD.

As a DIY enthusiast, I was naturally thrilled by this, and even filmed a complete video tutorial showing step by step how to upgrade the original SSD with a third-party drive. The video proved hugely popular, eventually racking up 500,000 views.

Video: How to Upgrade the M4 Mac mini SSD

Good times never last.

With the launch of the latest generation Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly onto the main board, completely removing the possibility for users to upgrade with third-party NAND modules after purchase.

The Mac mini has gone from being unquestionably the best value Mac to a considerably more expensive product. Not only has the base model price jumped from $600 USD to $900 USD, but the 2TB upgrade option has also risen from $800 USD to $1,000 USD.

Today, if you want to buy an M6 Mac mini with a 2TB SSD, you need to pay Apple $1,900 USD. An M4 Mac mini with the same configuration but with a 2TB aftermarket SSD upgrade, at the then cost of approximately $320 USD for the post-purchase upgrade, would set you back around $920 USD. Of course, prices have risen considerably since then, so a direct comparison between the M4 and M6 may not be entirely fair (do you see my humour?), but this price gap of a full $1,000 USD is due not only to Apple's aggressive price increases, but also to Apple removing the ability for users to upgrade themselves.

I can roughly guess why Apple raised the base Mac mini price by $300 USD; I can also understand the large SSD price increase. Affected by AI and other factors, the prices of components, SSDs and memory have all surged significantly. But none of this explains why Apple chose to solder the SSD onto the main board instead of retaining the user-replaceable design as before.

Top-rated comment from MaxM

They absolutely have the capability to do it, they just choose not to. Major markets and country blocs such as the EU, China and India must enforce strict regulations requiring manufacturers including Apple to adopt modular designs. These regulations should also extend to companies like Sony and Microsoft. Consumer protection is currently nothing more than lip service.

We can speculate, but the real reason behind Apple's decision to switch back to a soldered SSD may never truly be known. What we do know is that these computers are indeed considerably more expensive, and that's something of an understatement. Comparing an M4 Mac mini with a 2TB aftermarket upgrade to an M6 Mac mini with a 2TB factory upgrade, the price is a full 106% higher.

9to5Mac's Take

Finding a base model M4 Mac mini at a reasonable price on the second-hand market may be a little difficult, but if you do find one, in terms of its base performance, features and upgradeable SSD, it remains a truly outstanding computer.

The silver lining is that all Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, so you can easily connect high-speed external storage devices via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. I personally am quite fond of the Samsung T9, which provides a relatively affordable way to expand your storage.

What do you think is behind Apple's decision to remove the user-replaceable SSD design from the Mac mini? Do you have any unique theories? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
